idea.body: Dividing by a fraction asks how many of that fraction fit into an amount. To divide, flip the second fraction upside down, then multiply. 2/3 divided by 1/6 asks how many sixths fit into two thirds. Flip 1/6 to 6/1, then 2/3 x 6/1 = 12/3 = 4. Four sixths fit into two thirds, which checks out since 2/3 equals 4/6. Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 always makes the amount bigger, since you are counting how many small pieces fit inside it.

figure.alt: One bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 4 shaded, showing that 2/3 equals 4/6, so four pieces of size 1/6 fit inside it.

workedExample.prompt: A rover's fuel tank has 2/3 of a tank of fuel left. Each short trip uses 1/6 of a full tank. How many short trips can it make?
steps: Dividing by 1/6 means asking how many sixths fit into 2/3.
The rover can make 4 short trips.

figure.alt: One bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 4 shaded, showing that 2/3 equals 4/6, so four pieces of size 1/6 fit inside it.

ways.name: Flip and multiply
ways.when: Use this for any division by a fraction.
steps: Dividing by 1/6 means asking how many sixths fit into 2/3.
ways.trap: Flipping the first fraction instead of the second one.

figure.alt: One bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 4 shaded, showing that 2/3 equals 4/6, so four pieces of size 1/6 fit inside it.

ways.name: Match the denominator, then divide the tops
ways.when: Use this when the two bottom numbers already share a common multiple.
steps: Rewrite both fractions with the same bottom number: 3/4 becomes 6/8, and 1/8 stays 1/8.
Once the bottom numbers match, divide the top numbers directly: 6 divided by 1.
No flipping is needed once the denominators match.
ways.trap: Dividing the top numbers before the bottom numbers are made to match.

ways.name: Group the shaded pieces
ways.when: Use this when you want to see how many groups of the divisor fit.
steps: Cut a bar into sixths and shade 5 of the 6 pieces for 5/6.
Since 1/3 equals 2/6, group the shaded pieces into chunks of 2.
5 shaded pieces make 2 full chunks of 2, using 4 pieces, with 1 piece left over.
That leftover piece is half of a chunk, so the answer is 2 and 1/2, which is 5/2.
ways.trap: Counting the leftover single piece as one whole extra group instead of half a group.

figure.alt: A bar cut into 6 equal pieces with 5 shaded, grouped into two chunks of 2 and a leftover half, showing 5/2.

frames.caption: Group the shaded pieces into chunks of 2.
The leftover is half a chunk: 5/2.
